papers.title: How Does Psilocybin Affect Daily Life Experience and Behavior? Protocol For a Multimethod Ambulatory Assessment Study Within a Clinical Trial of Psilocybin for Depression
papers.abstract: Introduction: Although psilocybin has shown promise for treating depression, responses vary considerably, with some individuals experiencing limiting improvement and even adverse effects. Research has largely relied on assessments conducted at discrete time points, providing limited insight into how post-psilocybin change unfolds in everyday life. The Dial-In study aims to characterize daily-life processes associated with differential responses to psilocybin, including factors associated with improvement or worsening following challenging dosing experiences. Methods and Analysis: Dial-In is a prospective, observational, multi-method longitudinal study embedded within a clinical trial administering 25 mg of psilocybin to up to 141 adults with major depressive disorder. Ambulatory assessments combine ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and voice diaries for 14 days pre- and post- dosing, and passive audio sampling via the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) for three four-day periods to characterize everyday affect, behavior, reflections, and social interactions. Outcomes include depressive symptoms, psychological well-being, and psychedelic-related adverse effects assessed through eight weeks post-dose. Analyses will examine whether affective sudden gains and losses, social support, interpersonal conflict, conversational focus, reflection and rigidity predict differential outcomes. Additional analyses will test whether these factors moderate associations between challenging dosing experiences and clinical outcomes. Ethics and Dissemination: The project was approved by WCG Institutional Review Board, with Emory University relying on WCG as the reviewing board. All participants provide written informed consent. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific presentations.

papers.title: Investigating Indirect Genetic Effects on Neurodevelopmental Traits Across Development and Reporters: Triangulating Twin-comparison and Trio-PGS Approaches
papers.abstract: Polygenic associations with neurodevelopmental traits may reflect both direct and indirect genetic effects. However, evidence separating these effects is limited and mixed, and rarely spans development or reporters, or triangulates across methods. We triangulated twin-comparison and trio-based analyses in the Twins Early Development Study, using eight polygenic scores (PGS) and repeated parent, teacher and self-reports of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) traits from ages 4 to 26. Analyses included up to 7,259 offspring with observed or imputed parental genetic data. Both approaches consistently supported direct genetic effects of ADHD and ASD PGS on corresponding traits, whereas evidence for within-trait indirect effects was limited. Cross-trait indirect effects emerged for several PGS, particularly in parent reports, and some were unexpectedly negative. These findings suggest that within-trait polygenic prediction of ADHD and ASD traits mainly reflects direct rather than indirect genetic effects, whereas cross-trait associations reflect some indirect genetic effects.

papers.title: Mapping disordered eating symptoms in the ABCD Study through the Eating Disorder Symptom Index
papers.abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) are serious psychiatric conditions that typically onset during adolescence and are often marked by a chronic and severe illness course. Capturing ED symptoms as they emerge is critical for charting risk markers and associated outcomes to inform early intervention and treatment efforts. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD(R)) Study is one such key study that could accelerate these efforts, but has been limited to date by a lack of clear, clinically informed definitions capturing youth at risk for ED-related concerns. The current manuscript aims to address this gap by defining ED symptom indices (EDSI) with a reproducible framework developed in collaboration with ED researchers and clinicians to identify youth with patterns of ED symptoms and behaviors that approximate subthreshold and diagnostic-like presentations. We describe item-level definitions and decision rules used to construct the EDSI, which include symptom indices of anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and other specified feeding or eating disorders. We then compare youth meeting EDSI criteria with those identified by existing ED categorical definitions in ABCD Study data releases. By providing transparent definitions and analytical tools for identifying youth with potentially clinically meaningful ED behaviors, the EDSI framework aims to facilitate more reproducible and interpretable research related to EDs using the ABCD Study dataset, while also providing a structure to examine the emergence, persistence, and change of ED-like symptoms longitudinally across adolescence and into young adulthood in future research.

papers.title: Persistent or recurrent depression in young adults: associations with systemic inflammation and early life adversity.
papers.abstract: Background There is limited research on persistent or recurrent depression into young adulthood. We examined the prevalence of recurrent/persistent depression in young adults, and associations with childhood trauma/adversity and systemic inflammation, and if inflammatory markers mediated associations between childhood trauma and subsequent depression. Methods ALSPAC participants with ICD-10 depression assessments at ages 18, 24 and 30 were classified as never depressed, transiently depressed (one episode), or persistently/recurrently depressed ([≥] 2). Trauma/adversity from birth to age 16/17 was characterised by type, timing and burden. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured at ages 9, 16, 18 and 24. Analyses used multinomial logistic regression, linear regression and causal mediation models. Results Among 2,014 participants, 78.9% were never depressed, 15.0% had transient depression and 6.1% had persistent/recurrent depression. Trauma/adversity was more strongly associated with persistent/recurrent depression (RRR 3.17, 95% CI 1.98-5.06; FDR-P=6.2x10^-6) than transient depression, with a dose-response pattern and stronger associations for threat adversities. Middle-to-late childhood (11-17 yrs) emerged as a sensitive period for persistent/recurrent (RRR 2.85, 95% CI 1.47-5.52) and transient depression (RRR 1.85, 95% CI 1.25-2.73). Trauma/adversity was associated with modestly higher IL-6 at age 24 (all FDR-adjusted P < 0.05); CRP associations did not survive multiple-testing correction. Neither marker mediated trauma/adversity associations with persistent/recurrent depression. Conclusion Persistent/recurrent depression affects approximately 1 in 20 young adults. Childhood trauma/adversity, particularly during middle-to-late childhood, was associated with persistent/recurrent depression, but measured inflammatory proteins did not mediate this association. Further work is needed to understand biological mechanisms underlying the embedding early life psychosocial stress.

papers.title: Functional connectivity of reward and cognitive control networks predicts body mass index but not binge eating disorder in women
papers.abstract: Background Binge eating disorder (BED) is associated with obesity as well as behavioral and neurobiological changes in the reward and cognitive control systems of the brain. To better dissociate neural mechanisms of pathological eating behavior, functional connectivity (FC) analyses have shown promise. However, there is currently no replicable signature of BED derived from fMRI. Methods We investigated FC in 61 women with varying symptoms of binge eating. The three groups included 21 women with BED, 20 women with subsyndromal BED (subBED), and 20 controls without binge eating (noBE) matched in body mass index (BMI) and age. To identify neural signatures of BED and BMI, we used seed-based FC fingerprints (nucleus accumbens, NAcc, for reward and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dlPFC, for cognitive control) to predict group or BMI based on resting state and task-based (food bidding) FC. Furthermore, we explored spatial patterns of FC to quantify associations with BED and BMI. Results Both seeds of the reward and cognitive control networks robustly predicted BMI (rs = .33 - .46). The dlPFC seed predicted BMI across conditions (resting state: p=.002; task: p=.012) while the NAcc seed only predicted BMI based on task-based FC (p=.007). In contrast, FC failed to classify binge eating groups better than chance. Conclusions FC within reward and cognitive control networks primarily reflect obesity-related changes. Despite pronounced differences in eating behavior, BED could not be reliably dissociated from subBED or noBE using FC fingerprints. These results highlight challenges in identifying BED-specific functional markers.

papers.title: Menstrual Cycle Exacerbation of ADHD Symptoms in Adults: Common, Person-Specific, and Not Confined to the Luteal Phase
papers.abstract: Objective. Patients often describe menstrual-cycle worsening of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). We prospectively evaluated sample- and person-level cycle effects on ADHD symptoms and their independence from cyclical negative affect and pain. Methods. In an intensive longitudinal cohort (2019-2024), 106 naturally cycling adults meeting DSM-5 ADHD criteria on integrated assessment rated daily inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity (Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale-IV), negative affect, and pain (median, 41 days) and provided daily salivary estradiol and progesterone for ovulation coding and phase-aligned cycle time (PACTS). Generalized additive models estimated sample-level and person-specific cycle curves; robust cyclicity was tested against each participant's own time-shuffle null. Lab cognitive testing at four counterbalanced phases provided post hoc validation. Results. Sample-average cycle effects were significant yet small (<1% of daily variance), but 54% of 87 participants tested individually were robustly cyclical in ADHD symptoms (95% CI, 44%-64%; inattention 43%, hyperactivity-impulsivity 26%), more often with informant-confirmed ADHD (69% vs 36%). Among them, the cycle explained median 52% and 51% of symptom variance, a mean swing of 2.6 and 2.1 DSM-5 criteria. Most remained cyclical after adjustment for affect (68%) or pain (81%). Worsening most often peaked at and after menses rather than premenstrually; no cycle met prospective criteria for premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Hormones did not differ by cyclicity. Conclusions. About half of these adults with ADHD showed robust cyclical symptom change, mostly not reducible to cyclical affect or pain and usually outside the premenstrual window. Future work should test its stability and whether a DSM-5 cyclical specifier is warranted.

papers.title: Cortical brain changes from early to mid-adolescence in offspring at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
papers.abstract: Objective: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) emerge in late adolescence or adulthood. Offspring at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ) or BP (FHR-BP) are more likely to develop psychiatric disorders. Prior work from the Danish High Risk and Resilience (VIA) Study found sex-specific volumetric brain differences in offspring at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP aged 11-12 years. This study builds upon these findings by testing whether they reflect group differences in rate of change or stable group differences from early to mid-adolescence. Methods: This study investigated MRI data from offspring at FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population- based controls (PBC) at baseline (11-12 years; n=288) and follow-up (15-16 years; n=249). FreeSurfer longitudinal processing derived total brain volume, cortical measures, and intracranial volume (ICV). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-age interactions and sex-specific group effects, as well as associations with psychotic experiences (PE) and lifetime Axis-I mental disorders. Results: The analysis did not detect group-by-age interactions, indicating similar developmental slopes across groups. However, at both time points, males at FHR-SZ demonstrated reduced brain and cortical volumes compared to PBC and FHR-BP males. These effects were attenuated after adjusting for ICV, which was reduced in males at FHR-SZ. The analysis additionally detected volumetric reductions in males with PE, after controlling for risk status. Conclusions: These results extend the previous findings to ages 15-16 years, indicating group differences are stable and persist into mid-adolescence. Associations with ICV suggest early neurodevelopmental effects, and volumetric reductions in males with PE suggest convergent effects with FHR-SZ.

papers.title: Association of Outpatient Crisis Services with Emergency Department Revisits in Suicidal Youth
papers.abstract: Abstract Background and Objective: Pediatric emergency department (ED) visits for suicidal ideation and behavior have increased substantially, highlighting the need for scalable outpatient interventions that reduce recurrent ED use. We tested whether referral to outpatient crisis services was associated with fewer mental health-related ED revisits, hypothesizing that referred youth would have lower revisit rates than those receiving usual community care. Methods: We conducted a quasi-experimental study of 3,125 youth presenting with suicidal ideation or behavior to a large academic childrens health system between October 1, 2023, and August 31, 2025. Youth were referred to outpatient crisis services or community treatment (usual care) based on slot availability and clinician discretion. Propensity score modeling balanced demographic, clinical, and prior treatment characteristics between groups. Results: Among 3,125 qualifying index ED visits, 763 (24.4%) youth were referred to crisis services and 461 (14.8%) received [≥]1 crisis visit within 30 days. In intent-to-treat analyses, referral was associated with fewer mental health-related ED revisits at 90 days (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR], 0.67; 95% CI, 0.56-0.81) and 180 days (aIRR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.59-0.80). Associations were strongest among youth requiring short-term hospitalization (aIRR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.36-0.58) and those with moderate-to-high suicide risk (aIRR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.39-0.61). Findings were consistent in as-treated analyses. Conclusion: Outpatient crisis services were associated with substantially fewer mental health-related ED revisits among suicidal youth, with the largest reductions among youth with greater clinical acuity.

papers.title: Trends in Gambling-Related Primary Care Encounters in Brazil, 2014-2025
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of online gambling and sports betting has raised concerns about gambling-related harm and its implications for public health. However, nationwide evidence regarding temporal trends and patterns of health care utilization associated with gambling remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. We conducted a nationwide retrospective study using administrative data from Brazil's Unified Health System from 2014 through 2025. We examined primary health care records associated with pathological gambling (ICD-10, code F63.0) and gambling and betting (code Z72.6). We analyzed temporal trends, seasonal patterns, and geographic and demographic distributions, calculating annual encounter rates per 100,000 inhabitants. Gambling-related primary health care encounters increased substantially during the study period, with a marked acceleration beginning in 2022. By 2025, nationwide rates reached 1.46 encounters per 100,000 inhabitants for pathological gambling and 0.60 per 100,000 for gambling and betting. Increases were observed across all five Brazilian regions, with the highest rates in the South and Southeast. Recorded encounters increased across age groups and both sexes, particularly among adults aged 20 to 39 years. Rates were also elevated among adolescent males and older women. Time-series analyses suggested seasonal variation, with higher indices generally between April and October. Gambling-related encounters in Brazilian primary health care increased markedly from 2014 through 2025, particularly after 2022, with substantial demographic and geographic variation. These findings indicate increasing documentation of gambling-related conditions within a nationwide public health system and underscore the need for improved surveillance, early identification, and access to appropriate mental health care.

papers.title: Secondary Analysis of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity of priovi in Borderline Personality Disorder
papers.abstract: The digital therapeutic priovi has small average effects for borderline personality disorder (BPD). In this preregistered secondary analysis, we aimed to explore the heterogeneity and potential moderators of these effects. Adults received priovi plus treatment as usual or treatment as usual alone. At the 3-month primary endpoint (N = 528), model-based recursive partitioning showed heterogeneous effects on Borderline Symptom List-23 (BSL-23) change (p = 0.022) and on clinically relevant response (p = 0.007). Benefit was larger at higher baseline symptom load: a representative tree split on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 at a score of 23, and the higher-score subgroup had roughly twice the BSL-23 reduction (conditional average treatment effects -0.40 versus -0.19). Baseline BSL-23, depressive symptoms, and recent life-threatening events ranked as the leading moderators. Quartile calibration of predicted CATEs was weak and non-monotonic. The moderators are hypothesis-generating and should not guide patient selection without external validation.

papers.title: Patterns of Childhood Exposomes, White Matter Development and Behaviors Link to Future Cognition and Psychopathology in Youth
papers.abstract: Environmental exposures during childhood strongly impact individuals' cognitive and socioemotional development, and psychiatric vulnerability. However, childhood exposures rarely occur in isolation. Instead, they form a highly correlated 'exposome' whose multidimensional relationships with brain development and behavioral outcomes remain poorly understood. Elucidating the complex interplay between brain, behavior, and environment requires a multivariate approach. This study used regularized multiset canonical correlation analysis on longitudinal data from 8,113 preadolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study to characterize latent multivariate dimensions linking diverse environmental exposures, tract-wisely resolved measures of white matter (WM) development and integrity, and multi-domain behavioral phenotypes and relate them to concurrent and future psychopathology. Two distinct multivariate dimensions were identified exhibiting different exposure, WM development, and behavior patterns. The first linked greater socioeconomic resources to more advanced WM development, particularly in dorsal-association tracts, and superior cognitive performance. The second dimension linked stronger psychosocial support with higher WM integrity, more advanced development of limbic tracts, and lower levels of psychopathology. Longitudinal analyses revealed differential contributions of these dimensions to follow-up cognitive, socioemotional and psychiatric outcomes. Moreover, WM and exposomic variates in these dimensions moderated the effects of childhood adversity on transdiagnostic psychiatric disorder risk, in sex- and context-specific fashions. Together, these findings clarify how childhood environmental exposures and the linked WM developmental differences relate to cognition and psychopathology risk, potentially informing the identification of candidate neural targets for future interventions.

papers.title: The Antipsychotic Load (AP_Load2026): a normalised prescribed-dose index for schizophrenia research
papers.abstract: Background and Hypothesis Schizophrenia research routinely reduces antipsychotic treatment to a single number, but the available summaries disagree. Chlorpromazine equivalents, the WHO Defined Daily Dose (DDD) and the percentage of the licensed maximum (%BNFmax) rank the same patient differently, most of all for clozapine, whose dose-concentration relationship varies several-fold with sex and smoking. We hypothesised that referencing clozapine dose to a target individualised for sex and smoking would track plasma clozapine better than dose-proportional measures. Study Design In the Antipsychotic Load (AP_Load2026), each daily dose is expressed as a percentage of a reference dose, summed without a cap. Clozapine is referenced to a target individualised for sex and cigarettes per day, under two published anchor schemes, and other antipsychotics to a dose reconciling the WHO DDD and the licensed maximum. The clozapine term was tested against plasma clozapine (1316 assessments, 255 patients) with log-log mixed-effects models, and the non-clozapine reference against independently derived published doses. Study Results The individualised reference tracked plasma clozapine better than any dose-proportional measure (marginal R^2 0.249 vs. 0.166; deltaR^2 0.082, 95% CI 0.044-0.120). The scheme with the larger smoking correction fitted better (0.249 vs. 0.231), an ordering robust to quality-control variants and co-prescription. Of five candidate references for other antipsychotics, %BNFmax was the least consistent with external criteria. Conclusions AP_Load2026 is a transparent framework for normalising prescribed antipsychotic dose. Its clozapine reference is validated against a biomarker, whereas the reference for other antipsychotics is a calibrated convention at least comparable with existing alternatives. The index is particularly suited to treatment-resistant and clozapine-enriched cohorts.

papers.title: Proteomic profiling of postmortem prefrontal cortex identifies molecular signatures of borderline personality disorder
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by a severe pattern of symptoms including emotional instability, impulsivity, and unstable interpersonal relationships. A complex interplay between genetics and environmental factors has been hypothesized to be associated with the development of BPD. While neuroimaging studies have identified structural and functional changes in the brain, and genome-wide association studies described some first genetic risk loci, the neurobiological underpinnings of BPD remain poorly described. To better understand disease processes in BPD, we performed a molecular characterization of the prefrontal cortex (PFC), an important brain region for emotion and impulsivity regulation in BPD. Label-free brain proteomics was performed in postmortem human brain tissue in a sample of n=79, with a case group of n=36 individuals with BPD and a control group of n=43 individuals without BPD. Differential protein expression analysis suggested protein-level dysregulation of mitochondrial, immunological, and neuroplasticity pathways. Network analyses identified a BPD-associated co-expression module enriched for protein secretory and synaptic processes that is druggable with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Additional druggability analyses on protein-protein interaction networks and drug-repositioning analysis suggested VEGF signaling as a potential pharmacologic target in BPD. When we integrated BPD proteomic signatures with genomic and proteomic datasets of common comorbidities such as posttraumatic stress disorder and major depressive disorder, we observed a strong convergent overlap across disorders, with STX7 and RTN4 identified as conserved, differentially expressed proteins. Our study provides first insights into proteomic signatures of BPD in the brain, suggests potential pharmacological targets, and provides evidence for convergent protein signatures across BPD and common comorbidites.

papers.title: Neurotransmitter-specific polygenic scores dissect clinical heterogeneity in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a highly heritable psychiatric disorder characterised by substantial clinical heterogeneity. While global polygenic scores (gPGS) capture genetic liability to SCZ, their ability to explain clinical variability remains limited. Pathway-stratified polygenic scores (sPGS) offer a biologically informed approach to patient stratification. In this study, common genetic variants were annotated across five neurotransmitter (NT) signalling pathways -- acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine, {gamma}-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate (Glu), and serotonin. sPGS adjusted for sex and ancestry principal components, were calculated in two independent cohorts with different available clinical data (N=3,044 and N=645). By clustering top-decile individuals across the five sPGS dimensions, we classified patients into five mutually exclusive patient profiles, which were then evaluated for their associations with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) symptom dimensions, age at disease onset (AAO), and three-year clinical remission and treatment response. Although gPGS showed no significant association with clinical outcomes, some sPGS-derived profiles captured clinically relevant heterogeneity across cohorts. Patients assigned to the Ach profile exhibited higher overall symptom severity, particularly negative symptoms and general psychopathology. Patients within the Glu profile were characterised by more severe negative symptoms, earlier AAO, reduced three-year remission, and poorer treatment response. Similarly, the GABA risk profile was also associated with three-year remission rates. These findings suggest that NT pathway-specific polygenic profiling may capture clinically relevant variation overlooked by genome-wide approaches. By identifying genetic profiles associated with symptom severity, disease onset, and longitudinal outcomes, this framework could contribute to biologically informed patient stratification and inform future precision psychiatry approaches in SCZ.

papers.title: Effectiveness of AI-Supported Holistic Health Management Through PREVERY's Digital Health Promotion and Prevention Program: A Prospective Before-and-After Observational Study
papers.abstract: Background: There is an increasing strain on our healthcare system due to rising numbers of diseases related to chronic stress. One approach to combat these stress-related complaints is health coaching. However, personal health coaching is expensive and time costly, while digital offers can complement the already existing health coaching strategies. Therefore, this study investigates the effects of an AI-supported, digital health and prevention program. Methods: 253 participants were included in the study, with 113 being analyzed eventually. General stress experience and self-efficacy were assessed at baseline (T1), after six weeks (T2), and three months after the interventional phase (T3) via a Numerical Analog Scale (NAS) with values ranging from 0 to 10, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and the PsyCap Scale (CPC). Results: A significant time effect was observed for CPC and PSS. CPC increased significantly from T1 to T2 and T3 and remained stable between T2 and T3, while PSS decreased from T1 to T2 and increased again by T3. All pairwise comparisons were significant. There were also significant time effects for self-reported current health status, health literacy, health awareness, and self-efficacy, with values at T3 being higher than at T1 (for health awareness, this was already evident at T2; for self-efficacy, this was additionally evident between T2 and T3), while no time effect was found for motivation. Conclusion: PREVERY seems to be an effective prevention program to increase psychological capital together with self-reported current health status, health awareness, health literacy, and self-efficacy, while at the same time reducing perceived stress.

papers.title: A robust coordinated molecular response following trauma promotes recovery and protects against chronic pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms
papers.abstract: The biological mechanisms governing recovery versus chronicity of adverse posttraumatic neuropsychiatric sequelae (APNS) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized longitudinal molecular changes among trauma survivors across ten APNS domains, including pain, anxiety, and depression. Recovery across these diverse clinical outcomes was associated with a shared, temporally coordinated transcriptional signature, characterized by early innate immune activation, subsequent homeostatic and wound-healing processes, and later adaptive immune responses. In contrast, chronic APNS trajectories exhibited limited transcriptional remodeling. We derived and externally validated an RNA-based Recovery Score (RRS) capturing the shared molecular response underlying recovery. Higher RRS was associated with greater clinical recovery, elevated peritraumatic cortisol, and lower cumulative stress exposure. Drug-response profiling identified candidate compounds predicted to mimic recovery-associated transcriptional changes. Together, these findings support posttraumatic recovery as an active biological process and identify shared molecular pathways that may be harnessed to prevent multiple adverse posttraumatic outcomes.

papers.title: SHARED GENETIC ARCHITECTURE AND DIRECTIONAL ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY AND BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDERS: AN INTEGRATIVE GENOMIC ANALYSIS
papers.abstract: BackgroundAttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occur, but their shared genetic susceptibility and directional associations remain unclear. MethodsWe analyzed European-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR accounting for linkage disequilibrium and sample overlap (MR-LAP), Causal Analysis Using Summary Effect estimates (CAUSE), colocalization, and Sum of Single Effects (SuSiE) fine-mapping assessed genetic sharing and directionality. ResultsGenetic correlation was substantial (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci; 36 (75%) showed concordant directions in both phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation implicated axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and developing midbrain cells. ADHD-to-BPD MR was positive (22 instruments; inverse-variance weighted beta = 0.487, SE = 0.082, p = 3.27 x 10^-9), persisting after outlier removal, MR-LAP correction, and exclusion of two instruments at colocalized loci. Reverse MR was positive (five instruments; beta = 0.303, SE = 0.112, p = 6.83 x 10^-3) but heterogeneous and variant-sensitive. CAUSE favored directional over sharing-only models in both directions (delta ELPD = 6.98 and 5.92, respectively). SuSiE colocalization supported shared signals at rs17576773, rs9969232, and rs4727799. ConclusionsADHD and BPD exhibit extensive genetic overlap involving 48 shared loci and convergent evidence of directional associations. Findings across complementary methods more consistently support an ADHD-to-BPD relationship, suggesting that shared genetic susceptibility alone may not fully explain their co-occurrence.

papers.title: Rapid antidepressant effects of psilocybin without increased SV2A binding: baseline binding predicts response
papers.abstract: We report a pre-registered [11C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD). Synaptic loss has been implicated in MDD, and psychedelics induce synaptic remodeling in preclinical models within 24 hours, raising the possibility that psilocybins antidepressant effects involve increased synaptic density. We used the PET radioligand [11C]UCB-J targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) to test this in thirty-five participants with moderate-to-severe recurrent MDD randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25 mg psilocybin or 100 mg niacin placebo, both with psychotherapeutic support. [11C]UCB-J PET was performed 2-7 days before and 15 ({+/-}7) days after dosing. Despite significant clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, we found no evidence of a group-level increase in SV2A binding (VT or BPND) relative to niacin in the hippocampus or frontal cortex. In secondary analyses, higher baseline VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group; this survived FDR correction at Day 8 and Day 15 (two of three pre-registered timepoints). Change in VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive FDR correction. These findings indicate that substantial antidepressant improvement after psilocybin can occur without a detectable group-level increase in SV2A binding, while raising the possibility that baseline SV2A binding could help identify individuals more likely to respond.

papers.title: Co-production of an oral health intervention: Enabling Service Users with Severe Mental Illness to Learn about and Engage (SMILE) with Good Oral Health
papers.abstract: BackgroundPeople with severe mental illness (SMI) experience poorer oral health than the general population. They are less likely to visit the dentist or brush their teeth and face unique barriers to accessing oral health support. There is a limited number of oral health interventions for people with SMI, and there is no conclusive evidence on their effectiveness. An integrated oral health intervention delivered by mental health professionals in a community mental healthcare setting could offer a scalable option to oral health support for people with SMI. In this paper we report on the process of co-producing such an intervention in England. MethodsThe intervention development process was informed by Hawkins co-production framework. In this paper we report on stages 2 (co-production) and 3 (prototyping). Two online and two face-to-face co-production workshops took place (N=22) involving service users with SMI (n=6), mental health professionals (n=8) and dental health professionals (n=8). Two online patient and public involvement consultations, and a professional stakeholder meeting were held during the co-production process to provide feedback on the co-production process. The workshops informed the core components, format and content of the intervention. ResultsThe co-production process resulted in five intervention components: 1) Initiating a conversation about oral health, 2) providing advice to people with SMI on keeping their teeth and mouth healthy, 3) weekly tooth brushing text reminders, and 4) mental health professionals updating the care record to document the administration of this intervention. To support intervention delivery, we co-produced an intervention flowchart, an intervention leaflet for people with SMI, and a training manual for mental health professionals delivering the intervention. ConclusionWe co-produced an integrated oral health intervention to be delivered to service users with SMI in community mental health settings. The next stage of the research is a single-arm feasibility study to assess whether the intervention is acceptable to people with SMI and feasible to deliver within the NHS.

papers.title: Greater Stress Response Network (SRN) Connectivity is Associated with Higher Worry in Men and Women Especially in Later Life
papers.abstract: BackgroundLate-life anxiety is common and disabling, with pathological worry as a core feature. The Stress Response Network (SRN: amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, paraventricular nucleus), which modulates threat and stress reactivity, and its interaction with the Executive Control Network (ECN), anchored by the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation via top-down cognitive control, may underlie individual differences in worry severity. We hypothesize higher SRN connectivity to be associated with greater worry severity and that this relationship may be moderated positively by older age, and female sex. MethodsWe recruited older adults with varying worry. Resting-state fMRI was used to compute SRN connectivity and SRN-ECN connectivity. Regression models tested associations between connectivity and worry (PSWQ), anxiety (HARS), and rumination (RSQ), adjusting for age, sex, race, and education. Exploratory models examined age and sex moderation and associations with emotion regulation/suppression and cognitive function. ResultsAmong 131 participants who were [≥] 50 years old, with varying levels of worry severity, SRN connectivity was significantly associated with greater worry severity (B=23.51 (SE = 12.12), p<0.05), whereas SRN-ECN connectivity was not. SRN connectivity was lower with greater age (B=-0.003 (SE=0.001), p=0.04), yet older individuals reported greater worry than younger with comparable connectivity. Greater language domain cognitive function was associated with lower SRN connectivity but higher SRN-ECN connectivity, while greater overall cognitive function was associated with lower SRN-ECN connectivity. Women reported lower use of daily expressive suppression and higher performance across cognitive measures than men. Higher daily use of expressive suppression was not significantly associated with either connectivity measure. DiscussionSRN connectivity, rather than SRN-ECN connectivity, may serve as the primary neural correlate of worry, shaped by age and cognitive function.

papers.title: The cognitive profile of the schizophrenia-associated 3q29 deletion syndrome and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome
papers.abstract: 3q29 deletion syndrome (3q29del) and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome (3q29dup) are associated with a range of neuropsychiatric phenotypes, including impaired cognition. However, previous sample sizes have been small, and cognitive performance has not been systematically compared between 3q29del and 3q29dup. For both disorders, the impact of familial background on cognition is unknown. 3q29del is associated with high risk for schizophrenia; in the general population individuals at Clinical High Risk (CHR) for psychosis exhibit impaired cognition, but the relationship between CHR status and cognition in 3q29del is unexplored. Here we address these questions in the largest sample of 3q29del and 3q29dup ever evaluated. Individuals with 3q29del (n=103, 58.3% male), 3q29dup (n=38, 55.3% male), and controls (n=54, 42.6% male) were assessed with the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, 5th Edition (PPVT-5) and the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery (Penn-CNB). Total PPVT-5 scores and global, domain-level, and task-level Penn-CNB scores were compared across groups. Compared to controls, 3q29del participants scored an average of 24.6 and 22.9 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB, respectively (p<3E-16); 3q29dup participants scored an average of 18.8 and 14.2 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB (p<4E-6). In addition, 3q29del and 3q29dup exhibit unique profiles of cognitive deficits. To assess the impact of familial background on cognition, we evaluated unaffected relatives of 3q29del (n=140, 38.6% male), 3q29dup (n=25, 24.0% male), and controls (n=45, 11.1% male). The average familial shift on the Penn-CNB was 22.4 points for 3q29del and 16.7 points for 3q29 dup. Individuals with 3q29del+CHR exhibited greater cognitive deficits than 3q29del-CHR. These results demonstrate that both 3q29del and 3q29dup are associated with significant cognitive impairment and indicate that cognitive testing should be standard of care for individuals diagnosed with 3q29del or 3q29dup.

papers.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Brief Health Chatbot Acceptability Scale (CAS): A Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundConversational agents (chatbots) are increasingly used to deliver health information to middle-aged and older adults, a population in which the determinants of technology acceptance are known to diverge from those of younger users. However, acceptability is inconsistently defined and typically measured with ad hoc, unvalidated instruments. The psychometrically sound chatbot measures that exist assess usability rather than acceptability or were validated in student samples. ObjectiveTo develop and conduct an initial psychometric evaluation of a brief, 10-item health chatbot acceptance measure grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). MethodsTwenty adults (mean age = 52.8 years, range 28-81; 85% aged 40 or older; 75% female) enrolled in a sleep-application pilot usability study completed the 10 candidate items, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and sleep measures (PROMIS Sleep Disturbance 8a; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). We examined item performance, internal consistency (Cronbachs alpha), dimensionality (exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation), and convergent validity (correlations with the SUS). ResultsA two-factor structure emerged and was invariant across rotation methods, resulting in an Information Quality factor and an Acceptance factor (interfactor r = .39). All items loaded [≥] .60 on their primary factor; mean communality was .83. Subscale reliabilities were high (Information Quality = .96; Acceptance = .94; full scale = .93). Both subscales correlated with the SUS in the expected direction (r = .69 and r = .59), providing preliminary support for convergent validity. ConclusionsThe measure shows a coherent and theory-consistent two-factor structure and shows preliminary evidence of reliability and convergent validity. Given the small pilot sample, these results must be viewed as provisional but identify the measure as a candidate for formal validation in a larger, independent sample.

papers.title: Classical machine learning versus transformers for predicting daily psychological distress from passive smartphone sensing and self-report: a prospective cohort study
papers.abstract: ObjectiveWe test whether data collected from daily passive smartphone sensing and self-reports can predict daily significant psychological distress with meaningful potential clinical utility, comparing across best-in-class machine learning algorithms. MethodsIn this prospective cohort study, 169 community-dwelling adults completed baseline surveys followed by 7 days of passive smartphone sensing (accelerometer, GPS, power state) and end-of-day Brief Symptom Inventory-18 (BSI-18) assessments. Cases were defined as days (total n = 1,062) where participants psychological distress measured with the sex-specific BSI-18 Global Severity Index T-score was [≥]63 (prevalence 11.2%). Four classical models (artificial neural network, elastic net, support vector machine [SVM], extreme gradient boosting [XGB]) and four transformers (sensor-only or multimodal; standard or fusion architecture) were tuned, Platt-calibrated and evaluated on held-out participants (210 records, 25 cases) with participant-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). ResultsThe SVM (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.93), the multimodal fusion transformer (0.84; 0.69-0.95) and XGB (0.82; 0.63-0.94) discriminated best; sensor-only transformers performed at chance (0.49-0.50). At the default threshold of 0.50, elastic net logistic regression was the best classifier (sensitivity 0.56, positive predictive value 0.64). At 0.12 (near the outcome prevalence), the SVM detected all cases (negative predictive value 1.00), but positive predictive values were low for all models (0.13-0.26). Decision-curve analysis favored most models over treat-all and treat-none lines at thresholds between 0.05 and 0.25. Baseline survey items, mainly on functional impairment, had the largest feature importance. ConclusionsCompact classical models performed as well as transformers, which were considerably more computationally intensive. Decision-curve analysis supports further clinical exploration of these tools for triaging daily psychological distress, though our results suggest the relative value of psychosocial assessments and digital data should be carefully analyzed. External validation is needed before clinical use.

papers.title: Greater than the sum of its parts: A novel psychiatric multimorbidity metric applied to rare disease
papers.abstract: ImportanceRare genetic syndromes are often drivers of complex multimorbidity. However, current methods consider multimorbidity as the sum of chronic diagnoses, which does not account for subthreshold impairment. ObjectiveTo develop a quantitative multimorbidity score (MMS) for rare genetic syndromes that summarizes the neurodevelopmental and psychiatric multimorbidity landscape, including subthreshold symptoms, using 3q29 deletion and 3q29 duplication syndromes as hallmark examples. DesignWe developed a multimorbidity metric and applied it to cross-sectional data. Remote phenotyping from 2023-2026. In-person phenotyping from 2017-2020. SettingRemote phenotyping conducted at Rutgers University. In-person phenotyping conducted at Emory University. ParticipantsParticipants were 6 years of age and older. 3q29del and 3q29dup recruited from the 3q29 registry and direct referrals and contacts. Syndrome status confirmed by genetic report review. Typically developing controls recruited from community sources and ResearchMatch. Main Outcomes and MeasuresWe developed a quantitative MMS across five distinct domains of functioning, operationalized as the sum of z-scores across six standardized assessments. The MMS was calculated for each study participant and compared across groups. Within 3q29del, we evaluated the relationship between MMSs and Vineland-3 adaptive behavior. Results96 individuals with 3q29del (52.08% male, 18.01{+/-}11.47 years old), 28 individuals with 3q29dup (50.00% male, 20.82{+/-}13.64 years old), and 53 controls (41.51% male, 17.77{+/-}10.74 years old) were included. 3q29del and 3q29dup participants had significantly lower MMS scores compared to controls (3q29del mean=-8.22{+/-}4.67, 3q29dup mean=-6.47{+/-}4.66, control mean=1.36{+/-}2.35, 3q29del p<2E-16, 3q29dup p=4.89E-16). Within 3q29del, subjects with more severe multimorbidity had greater impairment in adaptive behavior (R2=0.589, p<2E-16). The quantitative MMS is more highly correlated with adaptive behavior than traditional diagnosis-based multimorbidity metrics (quantitative MMS R2=0.589, diagnosis-based multimorbidity R2=0.447). In a subset of 24 3q29del participants with longitudinal data (58.33% male, 13.17{+/-}9.08 years old at first evaluation, average time to follow up=5.17{+/-}0.87 years), the MMS is stable over time (R2=0.858, p=8.34E-8). Conclusions and RelevanceOur novel quantitative MMS is an improved metric for measuring psychiatric multimorbidity in high-risk populations, and accounts for the impact of subthreshold impairments. When applied to 3q29del and 3q29dup, it quantifies the individual burden of multimorbidity, is stable over time, and is associated with clinical outcome measures. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSIn rare genetic syndromes, can we develop a quantitative, holistic, cross-dimensional metric of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric multimorbidity? FindingsWe developed a novel quantitative multimorbidity score that synthesizes data across five phenotypic domains and applied it to cross-sectional data from 96 participants with 3q29 deletion syndrome, 28 participants with 3q29 duplication syndrome, and 53 neurotypical controls. More severe psychiatric multimorbidity was significantly associated with worse adaptive behavior, and quantitative and discretized versions of our score were more informative than counting diagnoses. MeaningOur novel quantitative multimorbidity score is more informative than traditional metrics and incorporates the impact of subthreshold symptoms, rendering a more complete picture of an individuals level of impairment.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic Functional Brain Alterations Across Familial and Phenotypic Risk Samples: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ImportancePsychiatric risk factors are often associated with multiple clinical outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether functional brain activation changes are shared across risk for mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders. ObjectiveTo determine which patterns of functional brain activation are shared across risk for different psychiatric disorders, defined using phenotypic (e.g., clinical) and familial risk paradigms, relative to control samples. Data SourcesPubMed and Web of Science were searched for task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies involving samples at risk for a mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder, published between January 2000 and July 2026. Study SelectionStudies published in English, with whole brain results, comparing a high-risk sample to a control sample, with a mean age of 30 years or less, were included. Of the 5,748 studies screened, 101 met selection criteria. Data Extraction and SynthesisPeak voxel coordinates from contrasts were extracted. Study quality was assessed using an adapted neuroimaging methods quality checklist. Peak coordinates were pooled within studies, and a random effects activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis was conducted using the Python package JALE. Main Outcomes and MeasuresStatistical maps of spatial convergence in task-related brain activation were computed across risk groups and within subgroups defined by disorder risk (mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder risk), ascertainment paradigm (phenotypic, familial), and task domain (cognitive, affective, reward). Statistical significance was assessed using permutation-based cluster-level family-wise error (cFWE) correction. ResultsThe studies included comprised 2534 high-risk participants and 2686 controls. Across psychosis, mood, and anxiety risk groups, there was a common area of functional activation in the left lateral prefrontal cortex (k = 319, p < .05 cFWE), reflecting greater activation in high-risk groups compared to controls. Approximately 30% of studies in each risk group contributed to this finding, reflecting both ascertainment paradigms and all three task types. Within the psychosis risk group, additional alterations were identified in the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior insula. Conclusions and RelevanceIncreased left lateral prefrontal activation was shared across risk groups despite methodological heterogeneity. This region supports higher-order executive functioning and undergoes prolonged maturation and this finding may represent a shared marker of vulnerability. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSAre there shared differences in functional brain activation across psychiatric risk states compared with healthy controls? FindingsIn this meta-analysis of 101 studies involving 2534 participants at elevated risk for psychiatric disorders and 2686 control participants, participants at elevated risk had greater left lateral prefrontal cortex activation across mood, anxiety, and psychosis risk groups. MeaningGreater left lateral prefrontal activation may reflect neural processes shared across psychiatric risk states.

papers.title: Beyond Perinatal Mood: Breadth of Psychiatric Symptoms and Delay Discounting as Correlates of Mothers' Relational Reports from Pregnancy Through Adult Children
papers.abstract: Maternal mental illness affects roughly one in five mothers in the United States, yet most evidence linking it to the mother-child relationship comes from the first postpartum year and relies on self-report measures of depression, anxiety, and stress. In 613 women spanning five family contexts -- pregnancy and mothers whose youngest child was aged 0-2, 3-12, 13-17, or 18 and older -- we examined twelve psychological constructs as correlates of mothers relational reports. Eleven were associated with relational reports individually; entered together, only three retained independent associations surviving false discovery rate correction: cross-domain psychiatric symptom burden ({beta} = -0.38), delay discounting ({beta} = -0.11), and orienting sensitivity ({beta} = +0.10). To our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed study linking delay discounting to maternal relational reports. Depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress, and negative affect fell to non-significance, and the symptom composite that displaced them contains none of those domains, indicating that breadth of psychiatric symptoms, not their type, tracked relational reports. A person-centered analysis converged: the latent profile with the poorest relational reports was defined by symptoms across multiple domains rather than by elevated stress alone. Associations varied across family contexts, though because each context used a different relational instrument, differences cannot be attributed to child age. These cross-sectional findings suggest that the psychological dimension most closely tied to maternal relational reports is broader than the perinatal mood constructs around which research and screening are organized, and that cross-domain symptom assessment warrants prospective evaluation as a complement to mood screening.

papers.title: The Feasibility, Acceptability, and Perceived Need for Suicide Initiatives for Children in UK Primary Schools
papers.abstract: BackgroundCurrently, there are no specific suicide prevention programmes for primary (elementary) schools within the UK. However, given the rise in suicidal thoughts and/or behaviours amongst children under 11 years, the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need for these programmes need to be assessed. AimsThis qualitative scoping study aimed to explore whether there is a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools and, if so, what these should look like. Sample(s) & Methods92 participants took part in the study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with mental health professionals (N= 22), school staff (N= 8), and parents of children who had experienced suicidal ideation, behaviours, or been bereaved by suicide (N=7). Focus groups were conducted with secondary school students (N= 36) and primary school students (N= 19) across 5 schools. Data were analysed using thematic framework analysis. ResultsThree main themes were identified: 1) the necessity of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, 2) barriers affecting delivery and potential solutions, 3) the transition period from primary to secondary school. ConclusionOverall, participants supported the need and acceptability of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, particularly due to the rising concerns about suicidality among younger children and evidence that suicide-related discussions are already occurring within peer groups. However, careful consideration needs to be given to ensure it is delivered in a safe and age-appropriate way, with a focus on dispelling myths, promoting help seeking, and increasing knowledge.

papers.title: Anticholinergic Medications and Health in Adults with Autism or Intellectual Disability
papers.abstract: ObjectiveContributors to autistic adults elevated risk for negative aging-related outcomes, including Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD), falls, and mortality remain underexplored. One candidate factor is exposure to medications with anticholinergic (AC) effects. Thus, this study assessed prevalence of medications with AC effects, and their associations with ADRD, falls, and mortality across four groups: autism-only, autism+intellectual disability (ID), ID-only, and controls. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2017-2019 US linked Medicare and Medicaid claims data for 40+ year-olds. Autism, ID, ADRD, and falls were identified using validated algorithms, and mortality was based on Medicare/Medicaid death indicators. Medications were coded using a comprehensive AC potency scale. AC medication exposure effects and interactions between AC potency and group were examined using modified Poisson regressions. Sensitivity analyses to address indication bias excluded persons prescribed antidepressant and/or antipsychotic medication(s). ResultsAll three clinical groups experienced significantly greater AC medication exposure (autism+ID: 92.5%>ID-only: 88.6%>autism-only: 80.0%) than non-autistic/non-ID controls (61.3%). Additionally, AC medications were more frequently associated with ADRD, falls, and mortality in all of these groups. Stepwise associations between AC potency levels and ADRD, falls, and mortality were found, and these effects were more prominent for persons with autism and/or ID relative to the control sample. InterpretationThis study provides a foundational examination of exposure to AC medication effects and their associations with aging-related outcomes in middle-age and older autistic adults and adults with ID. AC medication exposure represents one potential modifiable risk factor for negative aging-related outcomes in these groups.

papers.title: Feeling Too Much or Too Little: Alexithymia Moderates How Self-Reported Physiological Hyperarousal Shapes Risky Decisions
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmbodied cognition frameworks propose that physiological states shape decision-making, yet the contribution of sustained threat-related hyperarousal and individual differences in interoceptive integration remains poorly understood. This study examined whether self-reported physiological hyperarousal predicted Prospect Theory decision parameters: loss aversion ({lambda}), value sensitivity ({rho}), and choice consistency ({tau}); and whether alexithymia moderated these associations. MethodsSixty-eight healthy young adults (M age = 18.94, SD = 1.46; 85% women) completed the DASS-21 anxiety subscale as a measure of hyperarousal, the TAS-20 as a measure of alexithymia, and a 64-trial Mixed Gambles Task; individual Prospect Theory parameters were estimated via hierarchical Bayesian analysis. Moderation analyses were conducted using Hayes PROCESS macro with Johnson-Neyman probing. ResultsSelf-reported hyperarousal negatively predicted choice consistency and value sensitivity, but not loss aversion. Alexithymia moderated both effects through distinct conditional patterns: the self-reported hyperarousal-choice consistency association was significant only below a TAS-20 threshold of 51.05 (67.65% of the sample), reflecting monotonic buffering; the self-reported hyperarousal-value sensitivity association was significant within a bounded TAS-20 range (45.31-66.08), suggesting that intermediate alexithymia constitutes a zone of maximal vulnerability, though this model only reached trend significance and should be treated as exploratory. No effects emerged for loss aversion. ConclusionThese findings indicate that sustained hyperarousal could selectively degrade evaluative precision and decision consistency, while leaving loss aversion intact. Alexithymia may operate as a stage-specific, conditional moderator of the body-decision relationship.

papers.title: Peripheral immune biomarkers, brain imaging phenotypes and treatment response in major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients ({beta} = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants ({beta} = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram ({beta} = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings support astroglial involvement in MDD and link peripheral immune variation to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.
